To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in task-specific focal hand-dystonia (FHD), abnormalities in brain activation are observed during the preparation of movements, but not during movement execution.

1) in task-specific focal hand Dystonia (FHD), abnormalities are present during movement preparation, 2) these abnormalities are not related to the motor execution phase, and 3) the observed abnormalities are not related or associated with the presence of task-related dystonic posture.

1) FHD patients have a deficit of activation during movement preparation in premotor cortex, supplementary motor area and putamen; 2) the deficit is present in both hands, but is more pronounced in the affected hand; 3) the deficit is independent of task demands, and 4) the deficit is not related to dystonic posturing during movement execution.
